newsitem.title: UK: Metal trade lukewarm to Alcoa's LME probe call.
newsitem.headline: Metal trade lukewarm to Alcoa's LME probe call.

text.p: A call by Paul O'Neill, CEO of Alcoa the world's largest aluminium producer for a probe into the London market, drew a frosty reaction from traders and industry sources here.

O'Neill said on Thursday he plans to write a letter to the London Metal Exchange (LME) and the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI), asking them to look for ways to avoid manipulation in the aluminium market.
This follows his concerns over how 10,000 tonnes of aluminium was put on warrant last Friday into the LME Rotterdam warehouse, resulting in an overall inventory increase.
O'Neill said it was rumoured that Barclays Metals was the company that moved the metal.
Traders were somewhat bemused by O'Neill's comments, given that such stock/warrant movements take place quite often, not only in aluminium, but also in other metals.
"It is a bit rich...some of the biggest manipulators over the years have been the producers," one senior trader said.

He noted that there has been consistent speculation over the persistent falls in LME aluminium stocks this year. Since January, total aluminium stocks have fallen by 30 percent to the current level of 654,375 tonnes.

But not all of this metal is believed to be moving into consumption. Rather, it is moving off-LME warrant, but is still being stored and not registered in data anymore and there is a suspicion that some is being held by producer interests.
"This is a bit like the pot calling the kettle black," another trader said.

Only three years ago, the world's major aluminium producers, both in the West and the former Soviet Union, came together and agreed to cut production over 18 months - the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU).
"Why did they do that? It was to get prices up, and it worked. A lot of consumers were not happy about paying higher prices for their aluminiun, as I recall," he said.

Others said that the inventory movement in question may have been aluminium held off-market in a long-term consignment deal that reached its conclusion. "That metal is now on the LME - it can be sold or lent," one said.

Also, there have been big one-off movements in copper stocks this week, which have not raised any eyebrows. On Wednesday 17,025 tonnes were added to inventories, On Thursday 13,025 tonnes, and on Friday another 7,800 tonnes.

Traders said it was highly unlikely that that tonnage of metal was taken off ships and physically stocked in the various warehouses. Instead, copper has been sitting off-warrant, and simply registered to take advantange of the current high backwardation for cash metal.
To some extent, the LME is looking at the issue, with its stock data from October onwards due to record metal that has been taken off warrant but not yet shipped out of the warehouse.

Senior industry sources said that metal landed but not registered may eventually be treated in the same manner. However, it was important to remember that the LME was not the sole repository of world metal stocks.
"I don't think you could get total transparency of stocks, and it would not be commercially feasible anyway," one said.
Meanwhile, so far Barclays Metals has declined to comment on the issue. "We have no comment to make. We do not comment on press speculation," a senior Barclays Metals spokesman said.
The LME was unavailable for comment, while the IPAI was not in a position to respond.
